b41c59fcb2e0.before:
Title: Larkspur Beam 800
Description: Larkspur Beam 800

The Larkspur Beam 800 is a rechargeable front light for commuting on dark roads, unlit bike paths and busy city streets.

Most small bike lights throw a round spot of light that also shines straight into the eyes of oncoming riders and drivers. The Beam 800 has a shaped lens with a flat top edge, similar to a car headlight, so the light lands on the road ahead instead of in people's faces.

On lit city streets, the job of a front light is mostly to be seen, and 200 to 400 lumens is plenty. On unlit paths and country roads you need to see potholes, gravel and animals early, and that is where 600 to 800 lumens makes a real difference at commuting speeds.

A side window on each side of the lens adds visibility at junctions.

Runtime drops quickly on the highest mode, and it drops further in cold weather because lithium cells deliver less capacity below about 5 °C. If your light dies early, use a lower mode on lit streets, keep the light indoors between rides in winter, and charge it fully before long rides. A battery that has been stored empty for months can also lose capacity for good.

The Beam 800 has four modes: 800, 400 and 200 lumens, plus a daytime flash. Rated runtime is 1 hour 30 minutes on 800, 3 hours on 400, 6 hours on 200 and 24 hours on flash. It charges by USB-C in about 3 hours. It is rated IP64 for rain and weighs 118 g with the mount.

The Larkspur Beam 800 costs $59.

baf916977aa2.before:
Title: Larkspur Floor Pump
Description: Larkspur Floor Pump

The Larkspur Floor Pump is a steel-barrel track pump for keeping your tires at the right pressure at home. Checking pressure once a week is the single easiest way to prevent flats and make your bike roll faster.

A mini pump is made to fit in a bag for roadside repairs. It works, but it takes hundreds of short strokes to fill a tire and most have no gauge. A floor pump moves far more air per stroke, stands on the ground so you can use your body weight, and has a gauge so you know the actual pressure. Most riders keep a floor pump at home and a mini pump or CO2 inflator on the bike.

The dual head fits both Presta and Schrader valves without swapping parts. For a Presta valve, first unscrew the small tip on the valve and press it once to free it. Push the head straight on, all the way down past the threads, then flip the lever up to lock it. If the head pops off or leaks, it is usually not pushed on far enough, or it has been put on at an angle, which can bend the valve.

The gauge sits at the top of the barrel, where you can read it while pumping.

The pump reaches 160 psi (11 bar). It stands 68 cm tall, weighs 1.9 kg and has a 90 cm hose. In our tests it took 18 strokes to fill a 700 x 28 tire from flat to 80 psi.

The Larkspur Floor Pump costs $49 and has a two-year warranty. A replacement head seal kit costs $6.

96c105e5400c.before:
Title: Larkspur Fold 20
Description: Larkspur Fold 20

The Larkspur Fold 20 is a folding bike for commutes that mix riding with a train, bus or car. It folds down small enough to carry onto a crowded train and slide under a desk at work.

The Fold 20 folds in three steps. The frame hinges in the middle, the handlebar stem folds down, and the seatpost drops to lock the package together. There are no loose parts and nothing to remove. With a little practice most owners fold it without looking.

Magnets hold the two halves together when folded, and the bike can be rolled on its rear wheel like a suitcase instead of carried.

The 20 inch wheels make the Fold 20 quick to steer in traffic. The long seatpost and telescoping stem adjust for riders from about 150 to 195 cm. Mechanical disc brakes and an eight-speed derailleur give it the stopping and gearing of a full-size city bike.

A front carrier block on the head tube takes a bag that stays in place when the bike is folded. Fender mounts are included.

The Fold 20 weighs 11.6 kg. It folds in about 15 seconds, and the folded size is 60 x 80 x 36 cm. The maximum rider weight is 105 kg. Tires are 20 x 1.5 inch.

The Larkspur Fold 20 costs $749 and comes with a five-year frame and hinge warranty.

Title: Larkspur Gravel GX
Description: Larkspur Gravel GX

The Larkspur Gravel GX is a drop-bar bike for long commutes, weekend rides on dirt roads and loaded day trips. It is built to be fast on pavement and stable on gravel.

The Gravel GX has an aluminum frame and a carbon fork. The geometry is a little longer and lower at the front than a hybrid, but more relaxed than a road race bike, so it stays comfortable for an hour or more in the saddle.

Compared with a flat-bar hybrid, the drop bars give you several hand positions and a lower, more efficient position into a headwind. A hybrid is more upright and easier to see traffic from, which some riders prefer for short city trips. For a commute longer than about 15 km with a mix of roads and paths, a gravel bike is usually the faster and more comfortable choice.

There are mounts for full fenders, a rear rack and three bottles, so the Gravel GX can be a year-round commuter.

Wider tires let you run lower pressure for grip and comfort on loose surfaces. Tire clearance matters because you also need room for mud and fenders.

The Gravel GX ships with 700 x 40 mm tubeless-ready tires and has clearance for 700 x 45 mm tires, or 650b x 2.0 inch. With fenders fitted, the maximum is 700 x 40 mm. The drivetrain is 2 x 10 with a 46/30 crankset and an 11-36 cassette. Brakes are hydraulic disc.

A size 54 Gravel GX weighs 9.8 kg without pedals. The Larkspur Gravel GX costs $1,399.

1daf8466e88a.before:
Title: Preventing Bike Theft
Description: Preventing bike theft

Most bike thefts are quick and opportunistic. A thief looks for the easiest bike on the street, so the goal is to make yours harder to take than the one next to it. This Larkspur guide covers locking, parking and what to do if your bike is stolen.

Lock the frame, not just a wheel, to something solid that cannot be cut or lifted over, such as a fixed bike rack or a thick metal post. Put the U-lock around the frame and the rear wheel inside the rear triangle. Keep the lock off the ground, where it can be smashed, and fill the inside of the lock so there is no room for a lever. Add a cable or a second lock for the front wheel.

Busy, well-lit spots with foot traffic and cameras are safer than quiet side streets. Never leave a bike locked outside overnight if you can avoid it.

Report it to the police straight away, with the serial number, photos and a receipt. Register it as stolen on bike registries, tell your insurer, and check local online marketplaces and second-hand shops for the next few weeks.

A common rule is to spend about 10 to 20 percent of the bike's value on locks. Write down your serial number today; it is stamped under the bottom bracket on every Larkspur bike. The Larkspur Lock D9 costs $79 and resists bolt cutters. Most bikes are stolen from homes, garages and shared bike rooms, not only the street, so lock it indoors too.

44084e8d0a55.before:
Title: Larkspur Lock D9
Description: Larkspur Lock D9

The Larkspur Lock D9 is a hardened steel U-lock for commuters who leave their bike on the street every day.

A U-lock is the best mix of security, weight and price for most city riders. Thieves usually attack locks with bolt cutters, and a thick hardened shackle is much harder to cut than a cable or a thin chain. A heavy chain lock can match a U-lock for security and wraps around bigger objects, but a chain of the same strength weighs two to three times as much.

The D9 shackle locks into the crossbar at both ends, so a thief has to make two cuts, not one, to remove it.

The inside of the shackle is long enough to go around a frame tube and a bike rack or a thin post. It is too small for most lamp posts and trees, which is on purpose: a snug lock leaves less room for a jack or a lever.

The lock comes with three keys and a key number you can register with us for replacements. If the key gets stiff or hard to turn, especially in freezing weather, spray a dry PTFE lube into the keyhole and work the key a few times. Do not use oil, which collects dirt and can gum up in the cold.

In the Larkspur Cleaning and Lubing a Chain guide, check chain wear with a gauge every 1,000 km and replace the chain at 0.5 percent stretch on 11 and 12-speed drivetrains, or 0.75 percent on others.
6d34f770bef1.before:
Title: Cleaning and Lubing a Chain
Description: Cleaning and lubing a chain

A clean, lubed chain shifts better, runs quieter and lasts much longer. This Larkspur guide covers a quick routine that takes about ten minutes.

Wipe the chain with a rag while turning the pedals backward. If the chain is black and gritty, use a chain cleaning tool or a brush with a bike-specific degreaser, then rinse with water and let it dry fully.

Put one drop of lube on each roller on the inside of the chain while turning the pedals slowly. Turn the cranks for a minute so the lube works into the links, then wipe the outside of the chain firmly with a clean rag. The lube needs to be inside the rollers, not on the outside where it collects dirt.

Wet lube is thicker and stays on in rain, but picks up more grime. Dry lube stays cleaner but washes off quickly in wet weather. Many commuters use wet lube from autumn to spring and dry lube in summer.

A chain that squeaks after a wet ride has had its lube washed out. Wipe it dry and lube it again the same day, or rust will start on the rollers.

For daily commuting, lube the chain every 150 to 300 km, or after every ride in heavy rain. Do a full clean about once a month. Check chain wear with a gauge every 1,000 km and replace the chain at 0.5 percent stretch on 11 and 12-speed drivetrains, or 0.75 percent on others. The Larkspur Metro 7 chainguard keeps the chain cleaner, so it can go about twice as long between cleans.

f416cdb602aa.before:
Title: Your First Bike Commute
Description: Your first bike commute

Commuting by bike for the first time can feel like a big step. Most of the worry disappears after a week. This Larkspur guide covers the route, the gear and how to arrive fresh.

The fastest route by car is rarely the best by bike. Use a cycling map to find quieter streets and bike lanes, even if they add a few minutes. Ride the route on a weekend first so you know where the tricky junctions are.

You do not need to ride every day. Start with one or two days a week, or ride in and take transit home. Leave ten minutes earlier than you think you need.

Ride slower than feels natural, especially for the last kilometre, and let your body cool down before you arrive. Wear a light layer and carry your work clothes in a pannier instead of wearing a backpack. If your office has no shower, a pack of wipes, a small towel and a spare shirt go a long way. An e-bike removes most of the effort if your commute is long or hilly.

You need a bike in good working order, a helmet, front and rear lights, a good lock, and a way to carry things. Fenders are worth fitting if it rains where you live. A basic flat repair kit covers most problems on the road.

If you already have a bike, the basics, a helmet, lights and a lock, cost around $150 to $250. For example, the Larkspur Shell helmet is $89, the Beam 800 light $59 and the Lock D9 $79. Most commutes of 5 to 10 km take 20 to 35 minutes by bike.

Title: Fixing a Flat Tire
Description: Fixing a flat tire

Every rider gets a flat tire sooner or later. This Larkspur guide covers how to fix one at the side of the road and how to stop it from happening again.

Shift to the smallest rear cog, open the brake if it has a quick release, and remove the wheel. Push the tire bead into the center of the rim all the way around, then use tire levers to lift one side of the tire off. Pull out the tube.

Before fitting a new tube, run your fingers carefully around the inside of the tire to find whatever caused the flat. If you skip this, the same thorn or glass will puncture the new tube within minutes. Put a little air into the new tube so it holds its shape, tuck it in, and roll the tire back on with your thumbs.

Repeated flats almost always come from one of four causes: tire pressure that is too low, which lets the tube pinch against the rim; something still stuck in the tire; worn tires with thin tread; or rim tape that has slipped and exposes a spoke hole. Check pressure weekly and replace worn tires.

A basic kit is a spare tube, two tire levers, a patch kit and a mini pump or CO2 inflator.

Our Larkspur roadside kit costs $34 and holds a tube, levers, six patches and a mini pump. Most riders can change a tube in 10 to 15 minutes with practice. All Larkspur Metro 7 and Gravel GX bikes use puncture-belted tires, which in our tests cut flats by about half.

baa1726cb87a.before:
Title: Winter Commuting
Description: 

Riding through the winter is easier than most people expect, once you have the right clothes, lights and a bit of extra maintenance. This Larkspur guide covers the basics.

Dress in layers you can open or remove. You warm up fast on a bike, so start the ride feeling slightly cold. A thin base layer, a windproof jacket and a buff or neck warmer cover most days. Hands and feet get cold first, so wear windproof gloves or lobster mitts and wool socks. Below freezing, add a thin hat under your helmet and waterproof overshoes.

Wider tires at slightly lower pressure grip better on wet and slushy roads. If your route has ice that does not get cleared, studded tires are worth buying. They grip on ice where normal tires simply slide, and they are the most effective single upgrade for icy commutes.

Salt and grit eat chains, cassettes and brake parts. After salty rides, rinse the drivetrain and brakes with plain water, dry the chain and relube it with a wet lube. Check disc pads more often; they wear much faster in winter grit.

Use a bright front light and a rear light, charged every night.

Studded tires cost about $60 to $120 each and are noticeably slower on dry roads, so run them at 30 to 40 psi only for the icy months. Rinse after every salty ride and lube the chain at least twice a week. The Larkspur Beam 800 runs 1 hour 30 minutes on its highest mode, but expect 20 to 30 percent less below freezing. The Larkspur Metro 7 internal hub is sealed against salt.

b19cb69ab942.before:
Title: Choosing a Frame Size
Description: 

A bike that fits is safer, more comfortable and more fun to ride. This Larkspur guide explains how to choose a frame size, what to do when you fall between two sizes, and how to tell if your current bike is too big.

Your height gives a starting point, but leg length matters more for standover and saddle height, and torso and arm length matter more for reach. Measure your inseam standing barefoot against a wall with a book pressed up between your legs.

Reach is how far forward the handlebar is from the saddle. If your back aches, your hands go numb, or your arms are locked straight, the bike is probably too stretched out for you. A shorter stem or a handlebar with more backsweep can help, but a frame that is much too long is hard to fix.

If you are between two sizes, choose based on how you ride. The smaller frame is more nimble and easier to make longer with a longer stem. The larger frame is more stable and upright. For commuting, most riders between sizes are happier on the smaller frame.

For the Larkspur Metro 7, small fits riders 155 to 168 cm, medium 168 to 182 cm and large 182 to 195 cm. For the Gravel GX, size 50 fits 158 to 167 cm, 52 fits 165 to 173 cm, 54 fits 171 to 179 cm, 56 fits 177 to 185 cm and 58 fits 183 to 192 cm. You should have at least 2 cm of standover clearance. Larkspur offers a free size exchange within 30 days.

4abe88d5bd5d.before:
Title: Saddle Height and Knee Pain
Description: 

Saddle height is the most important fit adjustment on any bike. A saddle that is too low or too high is the most common cause of knee pain in new riders. This Larkspur guide explains how to set it.

With your cycling shoes on, sit on the saddle and put your heel on the pedal at the bottom of the stroke. Your leg should be straight. When you pedal normally, with the ball of your foot on the pedal, your knee will then have a slight bend at the bottom.

Pain at the front of the knee, around or under the kneecap, usually means the saddle is too low, so the knee stays too bent under load. Pain at the back of the knee usually means it is too high and you are overextending. Pain on the inside or outside of the knee is more often caused by foot position or cleat angle. Raise or lower the saddle in small steps of 3 to 5 mm and ride a few days between changes.

The heel method is quick but depends on shoe thickness. An inseam formula is more repeatable.

For the inseam method, multiply your inseam by 1.09 and measure that distance from the pedal axle, with the crank in line with the seat tube, to the top of the saddle. A second common formula is inseam times 0.883, measured from the center of the bottom bracket. At the bottom of the stroke, a knee angle of 25 to 35 degrees is the usual target. Larkspur bikes have seatpost height marks every 5 mm.

ba8a4a013889.before:
Title: Tire Pressure
Description: 

Getting tire pressure right is the cheapest upgrade you can make to any bike. This Larkspur guide explains how to choose a pressure and how to tell when it is wrong.

The number printed on the sidewall is a safe range, not a target. Wider tires hold the same load at lower pressure, and your weight matters as much as the tire size. Heavier riders and riders carrying a loaded pannier should add pressure.

If the bike feels harsh, skips over bumps and loses grip on rough corners, the pressure is too high. If it feels sluggish, squirms in corners, or you get pinch flats with two small holes side by side, the pressure is too low. Many riders assume harder tires are faster, but on real roads a slightly softer tire absorbs bumps instead of bouncing off them, and ends up rolling faster.

Tubes lose air through the rubber, so a tire can drop 5 to 10 psi in a week without a puncture. Check with a floor pump gauge before your first ride each week.

For a 75 kg rider, try these and adjust in steps of 5 psi. On 28 mm tires, 70 psi front and 75 psi rear. On 32 mm tires, 55 psi front and 60 psi rear. On 40 mm tires, such as those on the Larkspur Metro 7 and Gravel GX, 40 psi front and 45 psi rear. Add about 2 psi for every extra 5 kg of rider and luggage. The Larkspur Floor Pump reads accurately enough for this, and fills a 28 mm tire in 18 strokes.

1304b2be9547.before:
Title: Larkspur Haul
Description: Larkspur Haul

The Larkspur Haul is an electric longtail cargo bike. It is built to replace a second car for school runs, grocery shopping and commuting with a lot to carry.

A longtail carries its load on an extended rear rack behind the rider. Compared with a front box cargo bike, a longtail is narrower, rides and steers much like a normal bike, and fits through standard doors and bike paths. A front box bike keeps children in view in front of you and fits a bigger load, but it is wider, heavier and takes some practice to steer. For two children and a bag, a longtail is usually the easier bike to live with.

The rear deck takes up to two child seats, or seat pads with a wraparound handrail and footboards for older children. Wheel guards keep feet out of the spokes.

The Haul uses a mid-drive motor, which works through the gears. On a steep hill with a full load, shift down early to a low gear and use the highest assist level. A high cadence keeps the motor in its strongest range and stops it from overheating.

A dual-leg center stand holds the bike level while children climb on. Four-piston hydraulic disc brakes are sized for heavy loads.

The motor is 250 W nominal with 85 Nm of torque. The battery is 720 Wh, with a rated range of 45 to 80 km. The rear rack carries 80 kg, and the maximum total weight including rider is 200 kg. The drivetrain is 10-speed and the wheels are 20 inch. The bike weighs 34 kg.

The Larkspur Haul costs $3,899 including the rear handrail and wheel guards.

e6d53256b798.before:
Title: Larkspur Metro 7
Description: Larkspur Metro 7

The Larkspur Metro 7 is our everyday city bike. It is built for riding to work, school and the shops in normal clothes, in any weather, without much fuss.

The frame is aluminum with an upright riding position, so you sit high enough to see over parked cars and turn your head easily at junctions. The fenders, rear rack, kickstand and full chainguard come fitted from the factory, which means you can ride the Metro 7 home from the shop and commute on it the next morning.

We chose a seven-speed internal gear hub instead of a derailleur. The gears are sealed inside the rear hub, so road grit and rain do not reach them, and you can change gear while stopped at a red light. A hub needs far less adjustment than a derailleur and is hard to knock out of line when the bike is parked in a crowded rack. The trade-off is a little extra weight and a narrower gear range, which suits flat and rolling cities better than steep hills.

Hydraulic disc brakes stop the same way in the wet as in the dry. The tires have a puncture protection belt and a reflective sidewall stripe.

The Metro 7 comes in small, medium and large and fits riders from about 155 to 195 cm tall.

A medium Metro 7 weighs 13.4 kg with fenders, rack and chainguard fitted. Brakes use 160 mm rotors front and rear. Tires are 700 x 40c. The rear rack is rated for 25 kg.

The Larkspur Metro 7 costs $849 and includes a lifetime frame warranty and a free first service after 300 km.

The Larkspur Pannier 20 holds 20 litres and fits a 15 inch laptop. The Larkspur Pannier 20 weighs 1.05 kg. For the Larkspur Pannier 20, the top hooks fit rack tubes from 8 to 16 mm. The Larkspur Pannier 20 costs $95 and is sold singly.
72e6a1c8a458.before:
Title: Larkspur Pannier 20
Description: Larkspur Pannier 20

The Larkspur Pannier 20 is a waterproof rear pannier for carrying a laptop, a change of clothes and lunch to work.

A backpack is simple and goes anywhere, but on a bike it traps heat against your back and raises your centre of gravity. A pannier lets the bike carry the weight low on the rack, so you arrive with a dry back and the bike handles better. The downside is that you need a rack, and a pannier is less comfortable to carry around off the bike.

The Pannier 20 is made from a welded, coated fabric with a roll-top closure. Roll the top down at least three times and clip it for a full seal. A padded sleeve inside holds a laptop off the bottom of the bag.

The bag hooks onto the top rail of a rear rack and a lower hook clips to the rack's lower strut. If your pannier bounces or jumps off over bumps, the top hooks are probably set too wide for your rack tube. Fit the included reducer inserts for thin tubes, slide the hooks so they sit close to the rack stays, and set the lower hook so it pulls the bag tight against the rack. A bag that swings at the bottom will also rub your heel.

The Pannier 20 holds 20 litres and fits a 15 inch laptop. It weighs 1.05 kg. The top hooks fit rack tubes from 8 to 16 mm. A reflective strip runs along the back and a shoulder strap is included.

The Larkspur Pannier 20 costs $95 and is sold singly.

For the Larkspur Shell, measure around your head about 2 cm above your eyebrows with a soft tape, and choose the size that puts you in the middle of its range. The Larkspur Shell comes in three sizes: small fits 51 to 55 cm, medium 55 to 59 cm and large 59 to 63 cm. For the Larkspur Shell, a medium weighs 330 g. On the Larkspur Shell, the rear light gives 25 lumens and runs 6 hours on flash. The Larkspur Shell costs $89.
5707ebc75771.before:
Title: Larkspur Shell
Description: 

The Larkspur Shell is a commuter helmet for daily riding in the city. It has a built-in rear light, a small visor and a fit system that works with a hat underneath in winter.

Every Shell meets the CPSC and EN 1078 bicycle helmet standards. Inside the foam there is a thin low-friction liner we call SlipLayer. In an angled impact it lets the head move a few millimetres relative to the helmet, which is designed to reduce the rotational forces that are linked to concussion. A helmet without such a liner still protects well against direct impacts, which is what the standards test, but the liner adds protection for the angled falls that are common on a bike.

A helmet only protects you if it fits. Measure around your head about 2 cm above your eyebrows with a soft tape, and choose the size that puts you in the middle of its range. Once adjusted, the helmet should sit level, about two fingers above the eyebrows, and should not rock when you shake your head.

A rear dial tightens the fit in small steps, and the straps meet just below the ear.

The rear light is rechargeable and has steady and flashing modes. Eleven vents keep air moving on warm days.

Title: Larkspur Sprout 16
Description: Larkspur Sprout 16

The Larkspur Sprout 16 is a first pedal bike for young children who have outgrown a balance bike or are ready to ride without one.

Children are much lighter than adults, so a heavy bike is harder for them to handle than it looks. We kept the Sprout 16 light with an aluminum frame and fork, and gave it a low standover height so a child can put both feet flat on the ground when stopped.

The cranks are short and the handlebar is narrow, matched to the size of a four to six year old. The chain is fully covered to keep fingers and trousers away from it.

The Sprout 16 has two short-reach hand brakes and no coaster brake. A coaster brake, which works by pedaling backward, is common on kids bikes, but it makes it hard for children to find their starting pedal position, and it does not teach the hand braking they will need on every bike after this one. 43ddf48c5681.before:
Title: Squealing Disc Brakes
Description: Squealing disc brakes

Disc brakes can squeal, especially in the rain. This Larkspur support page explains the common causes and fixes.

Squeal is a vibration between the pad and the rotor. The most common causes are water, contamination and pads that were never bedded in. Rain and road spray put a film of grit and water on the rotor, and the brakes usually sing for the first few stops until the pads clean it off. That kind of noise is normal and goes away as the rotor dries.

Squealing that continues in dry weather usually means oil or grease has reached the pads or rotor, from chain lube, a bike cleaning spray or a fingerprint. Clean the rotor with isopropyl alcohol. Contaminated pads should be replaced.

New pads need to be bedded in to lay down an even layer of pad material on the rotor. Find a safe flat road, ride at about 20 km/h and brake firmly to walking pace, without locking the wheel. Repeat 10 to 20 times on each brake. Do not come to a complete stop with the brake held on while the rotor is hot.

Resin pads are quieter and bite well from cold, but wear faster, especially in wet grit. Sintered metal pads last longer and cope better with heat and rain, but are noisier.

Larkspur bikes such as the Metro 7 and Volt E1 ship with resin pads. In wet commuting, resin pads last about 1,000 to 1,500 km and sintered pads 2,000 to 3,000 km. Replace pads when the pad material is thinner than 1 mm. Larkspur replacement pads cost $18 a pair.

ab321b55d147.before:
Title: Wobbly Wheels and Truing
Description: 

A wheel that wobbles from side to side is out of true. It usually happens after a pothole, a curb or a fall, as spokes loosen or bend the rim slightly. This Larkspur support page explains how to check it and how to make small repairs at home.

Lift the bike and spin the wheel slowly. Watch the gap between the rim and the brake pads, or a fixed point such as a zip tie on the frame. A wheel that moves sideways is out of true. First check that the wheel is properly seated in the dropouts and the axle is tight, because a loose wheel can look like a buckled one.

You need a spoke key in the right size. Find the part of the rim that moves toward the rub. Loosen the spokes on that side by a quarter turn, and tighten the spokes on the opposite side by a quarter turn, working on two or three spokes around the wobble. Spin, check and repeat in small steps. Squeeze pairs of spokes to feel for any that are much looser than their neighbors.

If the rim is dented, cracked or badly bent, or several spokes are broken, a shop will need to repair or replace the wheel.

Aim for less than 1 mm of side-to-side movement. On disc brake bikes, rubbing is often the rotor, not the rim; a bent rotor can be straightened by hand. A spoke key costs about $8. Shops typically charge $20 to $40 to true a wheel. A replacement rear wheel for the Larkspur Metro 7 costs $139.

d75d1cd34b38.before:
Title: E-Bike Battery Care and Range
Description: E-bike battery care

The battery is the most expensive part of an e-bike to replace, and how you charge and store it has a big effect on how long it lasts. This Larkspur support page applies to the Volt E1 and the Haul.

Lithium-ion cells age fastest when they sit at a full charge or completely empty, and when they are hot. For daily commuting, charging to about 80 percent and recharging before the battery drops below 20 percent is gentler than charging to 100 percent every night. Charge to 100 percent when you need the full range for a long ride, and start riding soon after it finishes. Always charge at room temperature, never below freezing.

Cold batteries cannot deliver their full capacity, so range drops in winter even though the battery is not damaged. Store and charge the battery indoors and fit it just before you leave. The range comes back when temperatures rise.

If you will not ride for more than a month, store the battery off the bike, indoors, at 40 to 60 percent charge, somewhere between 10 and 20 °C. Check it every two months and top it back up to about half. Never store it empty; a deeply discharged battery may not wake up again.

Expect 20 to 30 percent less range near 0 °C than at 20 °C. A Larkspur battery keeps about 80 percent of its capacity after 800 full charge cycles if charged to 100 percent every time, and after about 1,200 cycles if usually charged to 80 percent. The Volt E1 charger has an 80 percent setting on its switch. A replacement 504 Wh Volt E1 battery costs $599.

19e3e9489af7.before:
Title: Gears Skipping and Indexing
Description: Gears skipping

When a derailleur bike skips, jumps between gears or will not shift cleanly, the cause is usually cable tension. This Larkspur support page explains how to fix indexing yourself with the barrel adjuster.

New shift cables stretch slightly during the first few hundred kilometres, which lets the derailleur drift out of line. Other causes are a bent derailleur hanger after the bike falls over, and a worn chain and cassette. If the chain skips only when you pedal hard, and especially on the smaller cogs you use most, the chain and cassette are probably worn out and adjusting will not help.

Shift to the smallest rear cog. Find the barrel adjuster, usually where the cable leaves the shifter or enters the derailleur. Shift up one gear. If the chain is slow to climb, turn the barrel counterclockwise a quarter turn to add tension. If it climbs past the gear or rattles, turn it clockwise. Keep shifting through all gears and adjusting in quarter turns until shifts are clean both ways.

If indexing will not stay put, the hanger may be bent, and a shop can straighten it with an alignment tool.

Check chain wear every 1,000 km. A chain replaced at 0.5 percent stretch will usually let a cassette last through two or three chains. A shop gear adjustment usually costs $20 to $40, and a hanger alignment about $25. Larkspur bikes such as the Gravel GX come with a free first service after 300 km, which includes an indexing check. The Metro 7 uses an internal hub, which rarely needs adjustment.

ca42a18ad475.before:
Title: Larkspur Volt E1
Description: Larkspur Volt E1

The Larkspur Volt E1 is a commuter e-bike for people who want to get to work without arriving tired, and who ride on a mix of city streets, bike paths and short hills.

The Volt E1 uses a rear hub motor. Hub motors are quiet, cheap to maintain and do not put extra wear on the chain and cassette, because the motor pushes the wheel directly. A mid-drive motor, which drives the cranks, climbs steep hills more efficiently and feels more natural, but it costs more and wears drivetrain parts faster. For a mostly flat or rolling commute, a hub motor is the simpler choice.

A cadence sensor turns the motor on when you pedal. There are four assist levels and a walk mode for pushing the bike up ramps.

Integrated front and rear lights run off the main battery. Fenders, a rack and hydraulic disc brakes come fitted. The battery locks into the down tube and slides out so you can charge it indoors.

Range depends on assist level, rider weight, hills, wind and temperature. Expect less range in cold weather and at the highest assist level.

The motor is 250 W nominal with 45 Nm of torque, and assist stops at 32 km/h (20 mph). The battery is 504 Wh and charges from empty to full in about 4.5 hours. Rated range is 40 to 90 km. In our own testing on a hilly 18 km commute loop at the second assist level, a 75 kg rider got 62 km from one charge. The bike weighs 23.1 kg including the battery.

The Larkspur Volt E1 costs $2,199 and includes a two-year warranty on the motor and battery.

Title: Larkspur Beam 800
Description: Larkspur Beam 800

The Larkspur Beam 800 is a rechargeable front light for commuting on dark roads, unlit bike paths and busy city streets.

Most small bike lights throw a round spot of light that also shines straight into the eyes of oncoming riders and drivers. The Beam 800 has a shaped lens with a flat top edge, similar to a car headlight, so the light lands on the road ahead instead of in people's faces.

On lit city streets, the job of a front light is mostly to be seen, and 200 to 400 lumens is plenty. On unlit paths and country roads you need to see potholes, gravel and animals early, and that is where 600 to 800 lumens makes a real difference at commuting speeds.

A side window on each side of the lens adds visibility at junctions.

baf916977aa2.before:
Title: Larkspur Floor Pump
Description: Larkspur Floor Pump

The Larkspur Floor Pump is a steel-barrel track pump for keeping your tires at the right pressure at home. Checking pressure once a week is the single easiest way to prevent flats and make your bike roll faster.

A mini pump is made to fit in a bag for roadside repairs. It works, but it takes hundreds of short strokes to fill a tire and most have no gauge. A floor pump moves far more air per stroke, stands on the ground so you can use your body weight, and has a gauge so you know the actual pressure. Most riders keep a floor pump at home and a mini pump or CO2 inflator on the bike.

The dual head fits both Presta and Schrader valves without swapping parts. For a Presta valve, first unscrew the small tip on the valve and press it once to free it. Push the head straight on, all the way down past the threads, then flip the lever up to lock it. If the head pops off or leaks, it is usually not pushed on far enough, or it has been put on at an angle, which can bend the valve.

The gauge sits at the top of the barrel, where you can read it while pumping.

The pump reaches 160 psi (11 bar). It stands 68 cm tall, weighs 1.9 kg and has a 90 cm hose. In our tests it took 18 strokes to fill a 700 x 28 tire from flat to 80 psi.

The Larkspur Floor Pump costs $49 and has a two-year warranty. A replacement head seal kit costs $6.

96c105e5400c.before:
Title: Larkspur Fold 20
Description: Larkspur Fold 20

The Larkspur Fold 20 is a folding bike for commutes that mix riding with a train, bus or car. It folds down small enough to carry onto a crowded train and slide under a desk at work.

The Fold 20 folds in three steps. The frame hinges in the middle, the handlebar stem folds down, and the seatpost drops to lock the package together. There are no loose parts and nothing to remove. With a little practice most owners fold it without looking.

Magnets hold the two halves together when folded, and the bike can be rolled on its rear wheel like a suitcase instead of carried.

The 20 inch wheels make the Fold 20 quick to steer in traffic. The long seatpost and telescoping stem adjust for riders from about 150 to 195 cm. Mechanical disc brakes and an eight-speed derailleur give it the stopping and gearing of a full-size city bike.

A front carrier block on the head tube takes a bag that stays in place when the bike is folded. Fender mounts are included.

The Fold 20 weighs 11.6 kg. It folds in about 15 seconds, and the folded size is 60 x 80 x 36 cm. The maximum rider weight is 105 kg. Tires are 20 x 1.5 inch.

The Larkspur Fold 20 costs $749 and comes with a five-year frame and hinge warranty.

Title: Larkspur Gravel GX
Description: Larkspur Gravel GX

The Larkspur Gravel GX is a drop-bar bike for long commutes, weekend rides on dirt roads and loaded day trips. It is built to be fast on pavement and stable on gravel.

The Gravel GX has an aluminum frame and a carbon fork. The geometry is a little longer and lower at the front than a hybrid, but more relaxed than a road race bike, so it stays comfortable for an hour or more in the saddle.

Compared with a flat-bar hybrid, the drop bars give you several hand positions and a lower, more efficient position into a headwind. A hybrid is more upright and easier to see traffic from, which some riders prefer for short city trips. For a commute longer than about 15 km with a mix of roads and paths, a gravel bike is usually the faster and more comfortable choice.

There are mounts for full fenders, a rear rack and three bottles, so the Gravel GX can be a year-round commuter.

Wider tires let you run lower pressure for grip and comfort on loose surfaces. Tire clearance matters because you also need room for mud and fenders.

The Gravel GX ships with 700 x 40 mm tubeless-ready tires and has clearance for 700 x 45 mm tires, or 650b x 2.0 inch. With fenders fitted, the maximum is 700 x 40 mm. The drivetrain is 2 x 10 with a 46/30 crankset and an 11-36 cassette. Brakes are hydraulic disc.

A size 54 Gravel GX weighs 9.8 kg without pedals. The Larkspur Gravel GX costs $1,399.

44084e8d0a55.before:
Title: Larkspur Lock D9
Description: Larkspur Lock D9

The Larkspur Lock D9 is a hardened steel U-lock for commuters who leave their bike on the street every day.

A U-lock is the best mix of security, weight and price for most city riders. Thieves usually attack locks with bolt cutters, and a thick hardened shackle is much harder to cut than a cable or a thin chain. A heavy chain lock can match a U-lock for security and wraps around bigger objects, but a chain of the same strength weighs two to three times as much.

The D9 shackle locks into the crossbar at both ends, so a thief has to make two cuts, not one, to remove it.

The inside of the shackle is long enough to go around a frame tube and a bike rack or a thin post. It is too small for most lamp posts and trees, which is on purpose: a snug lock leaves less room for a jack or a lever.

The lock comes with three keys and a key number you can register with us for replacements. If the key gets stiff or hard to turn, especially in freezing weather, spray a dry PTFE lube into the keyhole and work the key a few times. Do not use oil, which collects dirt and can gum up in the cold.

The shackle is 16 mm hardened steel. The inside size is 102 x 229 mm. The lock weighs 1.52 kg and comes with a frame mount. In our tests it resisted a 24 inch bolt cutter, and it took 58 seconds to cut through with a battery angle grinder.

The Larkspur Lock D9 costs $79.

Title: Larkspur Haul
Description: Larkspur Haul

The Larkspur Haul is an electric longtail cargo bike. It is built to replace a second car for school runs, grocery shopping and commuting with a lot to carry.

A longtail carries its load on an extended rear rack behind the rider. Compared with a front box cargo bike, a longtail is narrower, rides and steers much like a normal bike, and fits through standard doors and bike paths. A front box bike keeps children in view in front of you and fits a bigger load, but it is wider, heavier and takes some practice to steer. For two children and a bag, a longtail is usually the easier bike to live with.

The rear deck takes up to two child seats, or seat pads with a wraparound handrail and footboards for older children. Wheel guards keep feet out of the spokes.

The Haul uses a mid-drive motor, which works through the gears. On a steep hill with a full load, shift down early to a low gear and use the highest assist level. A high cadence keeps the motor in its strongest range and stops it from overheating.

A dual-leg center stand holds the bike level while children climb on. Four-piston hydraulic disc brakes are sized for heavy loads.

The motor is 250 W nominal with 85 Nm of torque. The battery is 720 Wh, with a rated range of 45 to 80 km. The rear rack carries 80 kg, and the maximum total weight including rider is 200 kg. The drivetrain is 10-speed and the wheels are 20 inch. The bike weighs 34 kg.

The Larkspur Haul costs $3,899 including the rear handrail and wheel guards.

e6d53256b798.before:
Title: Larkspur Metro 7
Description: Larkspur Metro 7

The Larkspur Metro 7 is our everyday city bike. It is built for riding to work, school and the shops in normal clothes, in any weather, without much fuss.

The frame is aluminum with an upright riding position, so you sit high enough to see over parked cars and turn your head easily at junctions. The fenders, rear rack, kickstand and full chainguard come fitted from the factory, which means you can ride the Metro 7 home from the shop and commute on it the next morning.

We chose a seven-speed internal gear hub instead of a derailleur. The gears are sealed inside the rear hub, so road grit and rain do not reach them, and you can change gear while stopped at a red light. A hub needs far less adjustment than a derailleur and is hard to knock out of line when the bike is parked in a crowded rack. The trade-off is a little extra weight and a narrower gear range, which suits flat and rolling cities better than steep hills.

Hydraulic disc brakes stop the same way in the wet as in the dry. The tires have a puncture protection belt and a reflective sidewall stripe.

The Metro 7 comes in small, medium and large and fits riders from about 155 to 195 cm tall.

A medium Metro 7 weighs 13.4 kg with fenders, rack and chainguard fitted. Brakes use 160 mm rotors front and rear. Tires are 700 x 40c. The rear rack is rated for 25 kg.

The Larkspur Metro 7 costs $849 and includes a lifetime frame warranty and a free first service after 300 km.

72e6a1c8a458.before:
Title: Larkspur Pannier 20
Description: Larkspur Pannier 20

The Larkspur Pannier 20 is a waterproof rear pannier for carrying a laptop, a change of clothes and lunch to work.

A backpack is simple and goes anywhere, but on a bike it traps heat against your back and raises your centre of gravity. A pannier lets the bike carry the weight low on the rack, so you arrive with a dry back and the bike handles better. The downside is that you need a rack, and a pannier is less comfortable to carry around off the bike.

The Pannier 20 is made from a welded, coated fabric with a roll-top closure. Roll the top down at least three times and clip it for a full seal. A padded sleeve inside holds a laptop off the bottom of the bag.

The bag hooks onto the top rail of a rear rack and a lower hook clips to the rack's lower strut. If your pannier bounces or jumps off over bumps, the top hooks are probably set too wide for your rack tube. Fit the included reducer inserts for thin tubes, slide the hooks so they sit close to the rack stays, and set the lower hook so it pulls the bag tight against the rack. A bag that swings at the bottom will also rub your heel.

The Pannier 20 holds 20 litres and fits a 15 inch laptop. It weighs 1.05 kg. The top hooks fit rack tubes from 8 to 16 mm. A reflective strip runs along the back and a shoulder strap is included.

The Larkspur Pannier 20 costs $95 and is sold singly.

5707ebc75771.before:
Title: Larkspur Shell
Description: 

The Larkspur Shell is a commuter helmet for daily riding in the city. It has a built-in rear light, a small visor and a fit system that works with a hat underneath in winter.

Every Shell meets the CPSC and EN 1078 bicycle helmet standards. Inside the foam there is a thin low-friction liner we call SlipLayer. In an angled impact it lets the head move a few millimetres relative to the helmet, which is designed to reduce the rotational forces that are linked to concussion. A helmet without such a liner still protects well against direct impacts, which is what the standards test, but the liner adds protection for the angled falls that are common on a bike.

A helmet only protects you if it fits. Measure around your head about 2 cm above your eyebrows with a soft tape, and choose the size that puts you in the middle of its range. Once adjusted, the helmet should sit level, about two fingers above the eyebrows, and should not rock when you shake your head.

A rear dial tightens the fit in small steps, and the straps meet just below the ear.

The rear light is rechargeable and has steady and flashing modes. Eleven vents keep air moving on warm days.

The Shell comes in three sizes: small fits 51 to 55 cm, medium 55 to 59 cm and large 59 to 63 cm. A medium weighs 330 g. The rear light gives 25 lumens and runs 6 hours on flash.

The Larkspur Shell costs $89. Replace it after any crash, or after five years.

Title: Larkspur Spin T2
Description: Larkspur Spin T2

The Larkspur Spin T2 is a smart direct-drive indoor trainer for riding at home through winter or on days when the commute is not an option. It connects to common training and virtual riding apps.

With a direct-drive trainer you remove the rear wheel and mount the bike on the trainer's own cassette. A wheel-on trainer is cheaper and quicker to set up because the bike keeps its wheel, but the tire slips under hard efforts, wears quickly and makes more noise, and the power reading changes with tire pressure. Direct drive is quieter, more accurate and feels closer to riding on the road.

The Spin T2 measures power with strain gauges and calibrates itself automatically. If its power reading does not match your bike's power meter, first check that both are calibrated. A spin-down or zero offset before the ride, after a 10 minute warm-up, fixes most differences. A gap of a few percent is normal because the trainer measures at the hub, after some power is lost in the chain.

The T2 fits 130, 135 and 142 mm rear spacing and comes with an 11-speed cassette fitted. The legs fold for storage.

The Spin T2 handles up to 1,800 W and simulates climbs up to 18 percent. Claimed power accuracy is plus or minus 2.5 percent. It weighs 16.8 kg and measured 59 dB at 250 W in our tests.

The Larkspur Spin T2 costs $749.

A gap of a few percent is normal because the trainer measures at the hub, after some power is lost in the chain.

The T2 fits 130, 135 and 142 mm rear spacing and comes with an 11-speed cassette fitted. The legs fold for storage.

The Larkspur Spin T2 handles up to 1,800 W and simulates climbs up to 18 percent. Claimed power accuracy is plus or minus 2.5 percent. It weighs 16.8 kg and measured 59 dB at 250 W in our tests.

Title: Larkspur Sprout 16
Description: Larkspur Sprout 16

The Larkspur Sprout 16 is a first pedal bike for young children who have outgrown a balance bike or are ready to ride without one.

Children are much lighter than adults, so a heavy bike is harder for them to handle than it looks. We kept the Sprout 16 light with an aluminum frame and fork, and gave it a low standover height so a child can put both feet flat on the ground when stopped.

The cranks are short and the handlebar is narrow, matched to the size of a four to six year old. The chain is fully covered to keep fingers and trousers away from it.

The Sprout 16 has two short-reach hand brakes and no coaster brake. A coaster brake, which works by pedaling backward, is common on kids bikes, but it makes it hard for children to find their starting pedal position, and it does not teach the hand braking they will need on every bike after this one. Our levers are sized so a small hand can pull them hard.

Removable training wheels are included. Most children who have ridden a balance bike will not need them.

The Sprout 16 fits children from about 100 to 120 cm tall, which is typically ages four to six. A five year old of average height, around 110 cm, is right in the middle of the range. Seat height adjusts from 50 to 62 cm. The bike weighs 7.2 kg.

The Larkspur Sprout 16 costs $329.

ca42a18ad475.before:
Title: Larkspur Volt E1
Description: Larkspur Volt E1

The Larkspur Volt E1 is a commuter e-bike for people who want to get to work without arriving tired, and who ride on a mix of city streets, bike paths and short hills.

The Volt E1 uses a rear hub motor. Hub motors are quiet, cheap to maintain and do not put extra wear on the chain and cassette, because the motor pushes the wheel directly. A mid-drive motor, which drives the cranks, climbs steep hills more efficiently and feels more natural, but it costs more and wears drivetrain parts faster. For a mostly flat or rolling commute, a hub motor is the simpler choice.

A cadence sensor turns the motor on when you pedal. There are four assist levels and a walk mode for pushing the bike up ramps.

Integrated front and rear lights run off the main battery. Fenders, a rack and hydraulic disc brakes come fitted. The battery locks into the down tube and slides out so you can charge it indoors.

Range depends on assist level, rider weight, hills, wind and temperature. Expect less range in cold weather and at the highest assist level.

The motor is 250 W nominal with 45 Nm of torque, and assist stops at 32 km/h (20 mph). The battery is 504 Wh and charges from empty to full in about 4.5 hours. Rated range is 40 to 90 km. In our own testing on a hilly 18 km commute loop at the second assist level, a 75 kg rider got 62 km from one charge. The bike weighs 23.1 kg including the battery.

The Larkspur Volt E1 costs $2,199 and includes a two-year warranty on the motor and battery.

Title: Larkspur Beam 800
Description: Larkspur Beam 800

The Larkspur Beam 800 is a rechargeable front light for commuting on dark roads, unlit bike paths and busy city streets.

Most small bike lights throw a round spot of light that also shines straight into the eyes of oncoming riders and drivers. The Beam 800 has a shaped lens with a flat top edge, similar to a car headlight, so the light lands on the road ahead instead of in people's faces.

On lit city streets, the job of a front light is mostly to be seen, and 200 to 400 lumens is plenty. On unlit paths and country roads you need to see potholes, gravel and animals early, and that is where 600 to 800 lumens makes a real difference at commuting speeds.

A side window on each side of the lens adds visibility at junctions.

Runtime drops quickly on the highest mode, and it drops further in cold weather because lithium cells deliver less capacity below about 5 °C. If your light dies early, use a lower mode on lit streets, keep the light indoors between rides in winter, and charge it fully before long rides. A battery that has been stored empty for months can also lose capacity for good.

The Beam 800 has four modes: 800, 400 and 200 lumens, plus a daytime flash. Rated runtime is 1 hour 30 minutes on 800, 3 hours on 400, 6 hours on 200 and 24 hours on flash. It charges by USB-C in about 3 hours. It is rated IP64 for rain and weighs 118 g with the mount.

The Larkspur Beam 800 costs $59.

baf916977aa2.before:
Title: Larkspur Floor Pump
Description: Larkspur Floor Pump

The Larkspur Floor Pump is a steel-barrel track pump for keeping your tires at the right pressure at home. Checking pressure once a week is the single easiest way to prevent flats and make your bike roll faster.

A mini pump is made to fit in a bag for roadside repairs. It works, but it takes hundreds of short strokes to fill a tire and most have no gauge. A floor pump moves far more air per stroke, stands on the ground so you can use your body weight, and has a gauge so you know the actual pressure. Most riders keep a floor pump at home and a mini pump or CO2 inflator on the bike.

The dual head fits both Presta and Schrader valves without swapping parts. For a Presta valve, first unscrew the small tip on the valve and press it once to free it. Push the head straight on, all the way down past the threads, then flip the lever up to lock it. If the head pops off or leaks, it is usually not pushed on far enough, or it has been put on at an angle, which can bend the valve.

The gauge sits at the top of the barrel, where you can read it while pumping.

The pump reaches 160 psi (11 bar). It stands 68 cm tall, weighs 1.9 kg and has a 90 cm hose. In our tests it took 18 strokes to fill a 700 x 28 tire from flat to 80 psi.

The Larkspur Floor Pump costs $49 and has a two-year warranty. A replacement head seal kit costs $6.

Title: Larkspur Fold 20
Description: Larkspur Fold 20

The Larkspur Fold 20 is a folding bike for commutes that mix riding with a train, bus or car. It folds down small enough to carry onto a crowded train and slide under a desk at work.

The Fold 20 folds in three steps. The frame hinges in the middle, the handlebar stem folds down, and the seatpost drops to lock the package together. There are no loose parts and nothing to remove. With a little practice most owners fold it without looking.

Magnets hold the two halves together when folded, and the bike can be rolled on its rear wheel like a suitcase instead of carried.

The 20 inch wheels make the Fold 20 quick to steer in traffic. The long seatpost and telescoping stem adjust for riders from about 150 to 195 cm. Mechanical disc brakes and an eight-speed derailleur give it the stopping and gearing of a full-size city bike.

A front carrier block on the head tube takes a bag that stays in place when the bike is folded. Fender mounts are included.

The Fold 20 weighs 11.6 kg. It folds in about 15 seconds, and the folded size is 60 x 80 x 36 cm. The maximum rider weight is 105 kg. Tires are 20 x 1.5 inch.

Title: Larkspur Gravel GX
Description: Larkspur Gravel GX

The Larkspur Gravel GX is a drop-bar bike for long commutes, weekend rides on dirt roads and loaded day trips. It is built to be fast on pavement and stable on gravel.

The Gravel GX has an aluminum frame and a carbon fork. The geometry is a little longer and lower at the front than a hybrid, but more relaxed than a road race bike, so it stays comfortable for an hour or more in the saddle.

Compared with a flat-bar hybrid, the drop bars give you several hand positions and a lower, more efficient position into a headwind. A hybrid is more upright and easier to see traffic from, which some riders prefer for short city trips. For a commute longer than about 15 km with a mix of roads and paths, a gravel bike is usually the faster and more comfortable choice.

There are mounts for full fenders, a rear rack and three bottles, so the Gravel GX can be a year-round commuter.

Wider tires let you run lower pressure for grip and comfort on loose surfaces. Tire clearance matters because you also need room for mud and fenders.

The Gravel GX ships with 700 x 40 mm tubeless-ready tires and has clearance for 700 x 45 mm tires, or 650b x 2.0 inch. With fenders fitted, the maximum is 700 x 40 mm. The drivetrain is 2 x 10 with a 46/30 crankset and an 11-36 cassette. Brakes are hydraulic disc.

A size 54 Gravel GX weighs 9.8 kg without pedals. The Larkspur Gravel GX costs $1,399.

1daf8466e88a.before:
Title: Preventing Bike Theft
Description: Preventing bike theft

Most bike thefts are quick and opportunistic. A thief looks for the easiest bike on the street, so the goal is to make yours harder to take than the one next to it. This Larkspur guide covers locking, parking and what to do if your bike is stolen.

Lock the frame, not just a wheel, to something solid that cannot be cut or lifted over, such as a fixed bike rack or a thick metal post. Put the U-lock around the frame and the rear wheel inside the rear triangle. Keep the lock off the ground, where it can be smashed, and fill the inside of the lock so there is no room for a lever. Add a cable or a second lock for the front wheel.

Busy, well-lit spots with foot traffic and cameras are safer than quiet side streets. Never leave a bike locked outside overnight if you can avoid it.

Report it to the police straight away, with the serial number, photos and a receipt. Register it as stolen on bike registries, tell your insurer, and check local online marketplaces and second-hand shops for the next few weeks.

A common rule is to spend about 10 to 20 percent of the bike's value on locks. Write down your serial number today; it is stamped under the bottom bracket on every Larkspur bike. The Larkspur Lock D9 costs $79 and resists bolt cutters. Most bikes are stolen from homes, garages and shared bike rooms, not only the street, so lock it indoors too.

44084e8d0a55.before:
Title: Larkspur Lock D9
Description: Larkspur Lock D9

The Larkspur Lock D9 is a hardened steel U-lock for commuters who leave their bike on the street every day.

A U-lock is the best mix of security, weight and price for most city riders. Thieves usually attack locks with bolt cutters, and a thick hardened shackle is much harder to cut than a cable or a thin chain. A heavy chain lock can match a U-lock for security and wraps around bigger objects, but a chain of the same strength weighs two to three times as much.

The D9 shackle locks into the crossbar at both ends, so a thief has to make two cuts, not one, to remove it.

The inside of the shackle is long enough to go around a frame tube and a bike rack or a thin post. It is too small for most lamp posts and trees, which is on purpose: a snug lock leaves less room for a jack or a lever.

The lock comes with three keys and a key number you can register with us for replacements. If the key gets stiff or hard to turn, especially in freezing weather, spray a dry PTFE lube into the keyhole and work the key a few times. Do not use oil, which collects dirt and can gum up in the cold.

The shackle is 16 mm hardened steel. The inside size is 102 x 229 mm. The lock weighs 1.52 kg and comes with a frame mount. In our tests it resisted a 24 inch bolt cutter, and it took 58 seconds to cut through with a battery angle grinder.

The Larkspur Lock D9 costs $79.

6d34f770bef1.before:
Title: Cleaning and Lubing a Chain
Description: Cleaning and lubing a chain

A clean, lubed chain shifts better, runs quieter and lasts much longer. This Larkspur guide covers a quick routine that takes about ten minutes.

Wipe the chain with a rag while turning the pedals backward. If the chain is black and gritty, use a chain cleaning tool or a brush with a bike-specific degreaser, then rinse with water and let it dry fully.

Put one drop of lube on each roller on the inside of the chain while turning the pedals slowly. Turn the cranks for a minute so the lube works into the links, then wipe the outside of the chain firmly with a clean rag. The lube needs to be inside the rollers, not on the outside where it collects dirt.

Wet lube is thicker and stays on in rain, but picks up more grime. Dry lube stays cleaner but washes off quickly in wet weather. Many commuters use wet lube from autumn to spring and dry lube in summer.

A chain that squeaks after a wet ride has had its lube washed out. Wipe it dry and lube it again the same day, or rust will start on the rollers.

f416cdb602aa.before:
Title: Your First Bike Commute
Description: Your first bike commute

Commuting by bike for the first time can feel like a big step. Most of the worry disappears after a week. This Larkspur guide covers the route, the gear and how to arrive fresh.

The fastest route by car is rarely the best by bike. Use a cycling map to find quieter streets and bike lanes, even if they add a few minutes. Ride the route on a weekend first so you know where the tricky junctions are.

You do not need to ride every day. Start with one or two days a week, or ride in and take transit home. Leave ten minutes earlier than you think you need.

Ride slower than feels natural, especially for the last kilometre, and let your body cool down before you arrive. Wear a light layer and carry your work clothes in a pannier instead of wearing a backpack. If your office has no shower, a pack of wipes, a small towel and a spare shirt go a long way. An e-bike removes most of the effort if your commute is long or hilly.

You need a bike in good working order, a helmet, front and rear lights, a good lock, and a way to carry things. Fenders are worth fitting if it rains where you live. A basic flat repair kit covers most problems on the road.

If you already have a bike, the basics, a helmet, lights and a lock, cost around $150 to $250. For example, the Larkspur Shell helmet is $89, the Beam 800 light $59 and the Lock D9 $79. Most commutes of 5 to 10 km take 20 to 35 minutes by bike.

0a8b4cbfd175.before:
Title: Fixing a Flat Tire
Description: Fixing a flat tire

Every rider gets a flat tire sooner or later. This Larkspur guide covers how to fix one at the side of the road and how to stop it from happening again.

Shift to the smallest rear cog, open the brake if it has a quick release, and remove the wheel. Push the tire bead into the center of the rim all the way around, then use tire levers to lift one side of the tire off. Pull out the tube.

Before fitting a new tube, run your fingers carefully around the inside of the tire to find whatever caused the flat. If you skip this, the same thorn or glass will puncture the new tube within minutes. Put a little air into the new tube so it holds its shape, tuck it in, and roll the tire back on with your thumbs.

Repeated flats almost always come from one of four causes: tire pressure that is too low, which lets the tube pinch against the rim; something still stuck in the tire; worn tires with thin tread; or rim tape that has slipped and exposes a spoke hole. Check pressure weekly and replace worn tires.

A basic kit is a spare tube, two tire levers, a patch kit and a mini pump or CO2 inflator.

Our Larkspur roadside kit costs $34 and holds a tube, levers, six patches and a mini pump. Most riders can change a tube in 10 to 15 minutes with practice. All Larkspur Metro 7 and Gravel GX bikes use puncture-belted tires, which in our tests cut flats by about half.

baa1726cb87a.before:
Title: Winter Commuting
Description: 

Riding through the winter is easier than most people expect, once you have the right clothes, lights and a bit of extra maintenance. This Larkspur guide covers the basics.

Dress in layers you can open or remove. You warm up fast on a bike, so start the ride feeling slightly cold. A thin base layer, a windproof jacket and a buff or neck warmer cover most days. Hands and feet get cold first, so wear windproof gloves or lobster mitts and wool socks. Below freezing, add a thin hat under your helmet and waterproof overshoes.

Wider tires at slightly lower pressure grip better on wet and slushy roads. If your route has ice that does not get cleared, studded tires are worth buying. They grip on ice where normal tires simply slide, and they are the most effective single upgrade for icy commutes.

Salt and grit eat chains, cassettes and brake parts. After salty rides, rinse the drivetrain and brakes with plain water, dry the chain and relube it with a wet lube. Check disc pads more often; they wear much faster in winter grit.

Use a bright front light and a rear light, charged every night.

Studded tires cost about $60 to $120 each and are noticeably slower on dry roads, so run them at 30 to 40 psi only for the icy months. Rinse after every salty ride and lube the chain at least twice a week. The Larkspur Beam 800 runs 1 hour 30 minutes on its highest mode, but expect 20 to 30 percent less below freezing. The Larkspur Metro 7 internal hub is sealed against salt.

Title: Choosing a Frame Size
Description: 

A bike that fits is safer, more comfortable and more fun to ride. This Larkspur guide explains how to choose a frame size, what to do when you fall between two sizes, and how to tell if your current bike is too big.

Your height gives a starting point, but leg length matters more for standover and saddle height, and torso and arm length matter more for reach. Measure your inseam standing barefoot against a wall with a book pressed up between your legs.

Reach is how far forward the handlebar is from the saddle. If your back aches, your hands go numb, or your arms are locked straight, the bike is probably too stretched out for you. A shorter stem or a handlebar with more backsweep can help, but a frame that is much too long is hard to fix.

If you are between two sizes, choose based on how you ride. The smaller frame is more nimble and easier to make longer with a longer stem. The larger frame is more stable and upright. For commuting, most riders between sizes are happier on the smaller frame.

For the Larkspur Metro 7, small fits riders 155 to 168 cm, medium 168 to 182 cm and large 182 to 195 cm. For the Gravel GX, size 50 fits 158 to 167 cm, 52 fits 165 to 173 cm, 54 fits 171 to 179 cm, 56 fits 177 to 185 cm and 58 fits 183 to 192 cm. You should have at least 2 cm of standover clearance. Larkspur offers a free size exchange within 30 days.

4abe88d5bd5d.before:
Title: Saddle Height and Knee Pain
Description: 

Saddle height is the most important fit adjustment on any bike. A saddle that is too low or too high is the most common cause of knee pain in new riders. This Larkspur guide explains how to set it.

With your cycling shoes on, sit on the saddle and put your heel on the pedal at the bottom of the stroke. Your leg should be straight. When you pedal normally, with the ball of your foot on the pedal, your knee will then have a slight bend at the bottom.

Pain at the front of the knee, around or under the kneecap, usually means the saddle is too low, so the knee stays too bent under load. Pain at the back of the knee usually means it is too high and you are overextending. Pain on the inside or outside of the knee is more often caused by foot position or cleat angle. Raise or lower the saddle in small steps of 3 to 5 mm and ride a few days between changes.

The heel method is quick but depends on shoe thickness. An inseam formula is more repeatable.

For the inseam method, multiply your inseam by 1.09 and measure that distance from the pedal axle, with the crank in line with the seat tube, to the top of the saddle. A second common formula is inseam times 0.883, measured from the center of the bottom bracket. At the bottom of the stroke, a knee angle of 25 to 35 degrees is the usual target. Larkspur bikes have seatpost height marks every 5 mm.

ba8a4a013889.before:
Title: Tire Pressure
Description: 

Getting tire pressure right is the cheapest upgrade you can make to any bike. This Larkspur guide explains how to choose a pressure and how to tell when it is wrong.

The number printed on the sidewall is a safe range, not a target. Wider tires hold the same load at lower pressure, and your weight matters as much as the tire size. Heavier riders and riders carrying a loaded pannier should add pressure.

If the bike feels harsh, skips over bumps and loses grip on rough corners, the pressure is too high. If it feels sluggish, squirms in corners, or you get pinch flats with two small holes side by side, the pressure is too low. Many riders assume harder tires are faster, but on real roads a slightly softer tire absorbs bumps instead of bouncing off them, and ends up rolling faster.

Tubes lose air through the rubber, so a tire can drop 5 to 10 psi in a week without a puncture. Check with a floor pump gauge before your first ride each week.

For a 75 kg rider, try these and adjust in steps of 5 psi. On 28 mm tires, 70 psi front and 75 psi rear. On 32 mm tires, 55 psi front and 60 psi rear. On 40 mm tires, such as those on the Larkspur Metro 7 and Gravel GX, 40 psi front and 45 psi rear. Add about 2 psi for every extra 5 kg of rider and luggage. The Larkspur Floor Pump reads accurately enough for this, and fills a 28 mm tire in 18 strokes.

1304b2be9547.before:
Title: Larkspur Haul
Description: Larkspur Haul

The Larkspur Haul is an electric longtail cargo bike. It is built to replace a second car for school runs, grocery shopping and commuting with a lot to carry.

A longtail carries its load on an extended rear rack behind the rider. Compared with a front box cargo bike, a longtail is narrower, rides and steers much like a normal bike, and fits through standard doors and bike paths. A front box bike keeps children in view in front of you and fits a bigger load, but it is wider, heavier and takes some practice to steer. For two children and a bag, a longtail is usually the easier bike to live with.

The rear deck takes up to two child seats, or seat pads with a wraparound handrail and footboards for older children. Wheel guards keep feet out of the spokes.

The Haul uses a mid-drive motor, which works through the gears. On a steep hill with a full load, shift down early to a low gear and use the highest assist level. A high cadence keeps the motor in its strongest range and stops it from overheating.

A dual-leg center stand holds the bike level while children climb on. Four-piston hydraulic disc brakes are sized for heavy loads.

The motor is 250 W nominal with 85 Nm of torque. The battery is 720 Wh, with a rated range of 45 to 80 km. The rear rack carries 80 kg, and the maximum total weight including rider is 200 kg. The drivetrain is 10-speed and the wheels are 20 inch. The bike weighs 34 kg.

The Larkspur Haul costs $3,899 including the rear handrail and wheel guards.

e6d53256b798.before:
Title: Larkspur Metro 7
Description: Larkspur Metro 7

The Larkspur Metro 7 is our everyday city bike. It is built for riding to work, school and the shops in normal clothes, in any weather, without much fuss.

The frame is aluminum with an upright riding position, so you sit high enough to see over parked cars and turn your head easily at junctions. The fenders, rear rack, kickstand and full chainguard come fitted from the factory, which means you can ride the Metro 7 home from the shop and commute on it the next morning.

We chose a seven-speed internal gear hub instead of a derailleur. The gears are sealed inside the rear hub, so road grit and rain do not reach them, and you can change gear while stopped at a red light. A hub needs far less adjustment than a derailleur and is hard to knock out of line when the bike is parked in a crowded rack. The trade-off is a little extra weight and a narrower gear range, which suits flat and rolling cities better than steep hills.

Hydraulic disc brakes stop the same way in the wet as in the dry. The tires have a puncture protection belt and a reflective sidewall stripe.

The Metro 7 comes in small, medium and large and fits riders from about 155 to 195 cm tall.

A medium Metro 7 weighs 13.4 kg with fenders, rack and chainguard fitted. Brakes use 160 mm rotors front and rear. Tires are 700 x 40c. The rear rack is rated for 25 kg.

The Larkspur Metro 7 costs $849 and includes a lifetime frame warranty and a free first service after 300 km.

The gears are sealed inside the rear hub, so road grit and rain do not reach them, and you can change gear while stopped at a red light. Hydraulic disc brakes stop the same way in the wet as in the dry. The tires have a puncture protection belt and a reflective sidewall stripe.

The Metro 7 comes in small, medium and large and fits riders from about 155 to 195 cm tall.

Title: Larkspur Pannier 20
Description: Larkspur Pannier 20

The Larkspur Pannier 20 is a waterproof rear pannier for carrying a laptop, a change of clothes and lunch to work.

A backpack is simple and goes anywhere, but on a bike it traps heat against your back and raises your centre of gravity. A pannier lets the bike carry the weight low on the rack, so you arrive with a dry back and the bike handles better. The downside is that you need a rack, and a pannier is less comfortable to carry around off the bike.

The Pannier 20 is made from a welded, coated fabric with a roll-top closure. Roll the top down at least three times and clip it for a full seal. A padded sleeve inside holds a laptop off the bottom of the bag.

The bag hooks onto the top rail of a rear rack and a lower hook clips to the rack's lower strut. If your pannier bounces or jumps off over bumps, the top hooks are probably set too wide for your rack tube. Fit the included reducer inserts for thin tubes, slide the hooks so they sit close to the rack stays, and set the lower hook so it pulls the bag tight against the rack. A bag that swings at the bottom will also rub your heel.

The Pannier 20 holds 20 litres and fits a 15 inch laptop. It weighs 1.05 kg. The top hooks fit rack tubes from 8 to 16 mm. A reflective strip runs along the back and a shoulder strap is included.

The Larkspur Pannier 20 costs $95 and is sold singly.

Title: Larkspur Shell
Description: 

The Larkspur Shell is a commuter helmet for daily riding in the city. It has a built-in rear light, a small visor and a fit system that works with a hat underneath in winter.

Every Shell meets the CPSC and EN 1078 bicycle helmet standards. Inside the foam there is a thin low-friction liner we call SlipLayer. In an angled impact it lets the head move a few millimetres relative to the helmet, which is designed to reduce the rotational forces that are linked to concussion. A helmet without such a liner still protects well against direct impacts, which is what the standards test, but the liner adds protection for the angled falls that are common on a bike.

A helmet only protects you if it fits. Measure around your head about 2 cm above your eyebrows with a soft tape, and choose the size that puts you in the middle of its range. Once adjusted, the helmet should sit level, about two fingers above the eyebrows, and should not rock when you shake your head.

A rear dial tightens the fit in small steps, and the straps meet just below the ear.

The rear light is rechargeable and has steady and flashing modes. Eleven vents keep air moving on warm days.

The Shell comes in three sizes: small fits 51 to 55 cm, medium 55 to 59 cm and large 59 to 63 cm. A medium weighs 330 g. The rear light gives 25 lumens and runs 6 hours on flash.

The Larkspur Shell costs $89. Replace it after any crash, or after five years.

Title: Larkspur Spin T2
Description: Larkspur Spin T2

The Larkspur Spin T2 is a smart direct-drive indoor trainer for riding at home through winter or on days when the commute is not an option. It connects to common training and virtual riding apps.

With a direct-drive trainer you remove the rear wheel and mount the bike on the trainer's own cassette. A wheel-on trainer is cheaper and quicker to set up because the bike keeps its wheel, but the tire slips under hard efforts, wears quickly and makes more noise, and the power reading changes with tire pressure. Direct drive is quieter, more accurate and feels closer to riding on the road.

The Spin T2 measures power with strain gauges and calibrates itself automatically. If its power reading does not match your bike's power meter, first check that both are calibrated. A spin-down or zero offset before the ride, after a 10 minute warm-up, fixes most differences. A gap of a few percent is normal because the trainer measures at the hub, after some power is lost in the chain.

The T2 fits 130, 135 and 142 mm rear spacing and comes with an 11-speed cassette fitted. The legs fold for storage.

The Spin T2 handles up to 1,800 W and simulates climbs up to 18 percent. Claimed power accuracy is plus or minus 2.5 percent. It weighs 16.8 kg and measured 59 dB at 250 W in our tests.

The Larkspur Spin T2 costs $749.

c946a6d27921.before:
Title: Larkspur Sprout 16
Description: Larkspur Sprout 16

The Larkspur Sprout 16 is a first pedal bike for young children who have outgrown a balance bike or are ready to ride without one.

Children are much lighter than adults, so a heavy bike is harder for them to handle than it looks. We kept the Sprout 16 light with an aluminum frame and fork, and gave it a low standover height so a child can put both feet flat on the ground when stopped.

The cranks are short and the handlebar is narrow, matched to the size of a four to six year old. The chain is fully covered to keep fingers and trousers away from it.

The Sprout 16 has two short-reach hand brakes and no coaster brake. A coaster brake, which works by pedaling backward, is common on kids bikes, but it makes it hard for children to find their starting pedal position, and it does not teach the hand braking they will need on every bike after this one. Our levers are sized so a small hand can pull them hard.

Removable training wheels are included. Most children who have ridden a balance bike will not need them.

The Sprout 16 fits children from about 100 to 120 cm tall, which is typically ages four to six. A five year old of average height, around 110 cm, is right in the middle of the range. Seat height adjusts from 50 to 62 cm. The bike weighs 7.2 kg.

The Larkspur Sprout 16 costs $329.

43ddf48c5681.before:
Title: Squealing Disc Brakes
Description: Squealing disc brakes

Disc brakes can squeal, especially in the rain. This Larkspur support page explains the common causes and fixes.

Squeal is a vibration between the pad and the rotor. The most common causes are water, contamination and pads that were never bedded in. Rain and road spray put a film of grit and water on the rotor, and the brakes usually sing for the first few stops until the pads clean it off. That kind of noise is normal and goes away as the rotor dries.

Squealing that continues in dry weather usually means oil or grease has reached the pads or rotor, from chain lube, a bike cleaning spray or a fingerprint. Clean the rotor with isopropyl alcohol. Contaminated pads should be replaced.

New pads need to be bedded in to lay down an even layer of pad material on the rotor. Find a safe flat road, ride at about 20 km/h and brake firmly to walking pace, without locking the wheel. Repeat 10 to 20 times on each brake. Do not come to a complete stop with the brake held on while the rotor is hot.

Resin pads are quieter and bite well from cold, but wear faster, especially in wet grit. Sintered metal pads last longer and cope better with heat and rain, but are noisier.

Larkspur bikes such as the Metro 7 and Volt E1 ship with resin pads. In wet commuting, resin pads last about 1,000 to 1,500 km and sintered pads 2,000 to 3,000 km. Replace pads when the pad material is thinner than 1 mm. Larkspur replacement pads cost $18 a pair.
